subject: religious-studies
title: Evil and Religious Experience
welcome_lead: Cover two further staples: theodicy and the argument from religious experience.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the problem of evil and religious experience.
final_note: Suffering and encounter test classical theism in opposite directions.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Augustine (354-430) accounts for evil as the privation of good arising from the misuse of free will. Irenaeus (c. 130-202), developed by Hick (1966), sees humans as created immature, with evil as the context for soul-making.

Plantinga (1974) defends the logical coherence of free will against Mackie's inconsistent triad.

William James' Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) studies mysticism empirically. Rudolf Otto's The Idea of the Holy (1917) names the numinous as a unique religious category.

Richard Swinburne defends the cognitive significance of such experiences through his principles of credulity and testimony.

Critics like Bertrand Russell and J.L. Mackie argue that religious experience admits naturalistic explanation (e.g. psychological, neurological).

Defenders reply that this is to confuse mechanism with meaning: showing how an experience occurs does not show that it lacks veridical content.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.
The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.
Religious experiences only happen during dreams.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.

options: Religious experiences are just hallucinations caused by stress.
Religious experiences only happen during dreams.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
Ineffability (beyond words), noetic quality (gives knowledge), transience (temporary), and passivity (feeling acted upon by something greater).

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
